# The cost of making a claim uncheckable

**Candidate C004 · Development draft · 22 October 2026**

**Originality verdict:** Generic duties to preserve evidence or remain corrigible are not new. The narrower candidate concerns transferring the cost of future correction when an institution withdraws a checking route on which it has induced reliance. Develop together with C085.

## A justified conclusion and a later decision

A public laboratory certifies that a construction material passes a specified safety test. Its evidence is currently good. Builders reasonably rely on the certification, and retaining every physical sample forever would be expensive. Five years later the laboratory proposes to destroy the remaining samples. No new reason to doubt the certification has appeared.

One question is whether the laboratory should believe its original conclusion. Another is whether it should conduct a new test now. A third is whether it may eliminate the only affordable means by which other people could investigate an important future challenge. The answers need not coincide.

The proposed thesis concerns the third question. An institution can be justified in retaining its belief and in ending active inquiry while owing preservation, replacement, or fair transfer of a route for correction. The duty arises here from continuing, foreseeable reliance together with control over an otherwise inaccessible means of checking. It does not follow merely from the abstract possibility of error.

## Two ways of closing the archive

Suppose the laboratory can retain a representative set of samples at modest cost. Alternatively, it can destroy them and leave every building owner to purchase invasive testing of installed material if doubt later emerges. That second route is physically possible but prohibitively expensive for many owners. The proposed destruction therefore does more than save the laboratory money: it transfers the prospective cost of correcting its own authoritative assurance onto those who relied on it.

Now change the case. The laboratory can send equivalent samples and adequate records to an independent archive with guaranteed access. Destruction of its own copies no longer creates the same problem. What matters is the checking capacity, not the continued existence of every original object.

This comparison suggests a replacement principle. When an institution permissibly retires a means of checking a claim on which it has induced substantial continuing reliance, it should normally preserve an adequate substitute or fairly provide for the additional burdens its retirement creates. Whether it must do so depends on the stakes, cost, availability of alternatives, duration of reliance, and competing claims such as privacy.

## Why reliance matters

There are many things one could learn more about. No person or institution can preserve every path to every possible discovery. Reliance narrows the duty because the institution has made its conclusion part of other people's practical arrangements. Those people may have forgone independent testing precisely because the institution occupied an authoritative role.

The principle is strongest when the assurance invited such dependence, the reliance was reasonable, the consequences remain significant, and the institution is uniquely positioned to maintain the route. It is weaker for casual conversation, trivial claims, or reliance the speaker neither invited nor could reasonably foresee. It may end when the relevant reliance ends. An institution cannot necessarily end it by announcing that it no longer wishes to be responsible while people remain trapped in the arrangements it encouraged.

The duty is best understood as moral and institutional, with an epistemic object. Calling it distinctively epistemic would require a further argument. Nothing here depends on proving that all responsibilities concerning inquiry arise from an autonomous epistemic norm.

## Existing work and the actual gap

Flores and Woodard's *Epistemic norms on evidence-gathering* (2023) already challenges a restriction of epistemic evaluation to responses to evidence presently held. Longino's *How Values Can Be Good for Science* (2004), pp. 133–135, already connects responsible inquiry with effective criticism and recognizes later reassessment. Neither broad expansion is available as our contribution.

The closest unresolved obstacle is Porat and Stein's *Liability for Uncertainty: Making Evidential Damage Actionable* (1997). Its abstract and publication record concern responsibility for damaging another's evidential position. I could not obtain the full text. The proposed replacement principle may turn out to be a prospective application of its existing argument. That would change the novelty assessment substantially.

The possible increment is thus narrowly specified: a duty can arise before any dispute, without negligent destruction or a present duty to collect additional evidence, because retiring an institutionally supplied checking route reallocates the cost of future correction. A useful essay must show why existing evidential-damage and reliance principles do not already settle precisely that case.

## Hard cases

One objection is that the probability of future error may be minute. The response is proportionality, not an unlimited preservation command. A cheap safeguard against a grave, durable risk may be warranted; an expensive safeguard against a negligible inconvenience may not be. No numerical threshold is supplied here, and the draft should not pretend to have solved that allocation problem.

A second objection concerns confidential records. An archive can itself harm people. Preserving correction may require a different route: controlled access, independent testing, or a restricted record sufficient for a particular challenge. Sometimes the privacy cost defeats preservation altogether. The principle then requires an honest account of the lost checking capacity rather than a fictional claim that nothing epistemically significant has changed.

A third objection is that induced reliance can be unreasonable. Someone who treats a clearly limited exploratory result as an unconditional guarantee does not automatically acquire a perpetual claim to laboratory resources. The assurance's content and reasonable use must be established independently.

## What survives

The worthwhile proposal is not “keep evidence.” It is a responsibility for shifting the future cost of checking an authoritative claim. C085 asks what happens once a challenge is raised; this draft asks what capacity must remain available beforehand. Those are complementary stages of one argument. They should not be counted as two independent discoveries.

### References and access

- Flores, Carolina, and Elise Woodard. 2023. “Epistemic norms on evidence-gathering.” *Philosophical Studies* 180:2547–2571. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11098-023-01978-8. Relevant opening arguments read.
- Longino, Helen E. 2004. “How Values Can Be Good for Science.” In *Science, Values, and Objectivity*, pp. 127–142. https://www.ugr.es/~zink/mono/Longino2004.pdf. Especially pp. 133–135 read.
- Porat, Ariel, and Alex Stein. 1997. “Liability for Uncertainty: Making Evidential Damage Actionable.” *Cardozo Law Review* 18:1891–1960. https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=10261. Abstract/metadata only; full text requested.
